Florence, September. Bellini is writing a book about the 1966 flood, for the sixtieth anniversary in November. He gives Pietro the first chapter to read and asks his opinion.
Well? Be honest. Is it boring?
No, it's wonderful. But why do you write everything in the passato remoto? "Ernesto aprì la porta", "l'acqua entrò"…
Because it's a story, not a letter. In books you use the passato remoto, even in Milan.
And this sentence? "Quando l'acqua ebbe smesso di salire, Ernesto scese in strada." "Ebbe smesso"? I've never heard it.
It's the trapassato remoto. It's used only in books, after "quando", "appena", "dopo che", if the main verb is in the passato remoto.
So first the water stopped rising, and straight after that he went down.
Exactly. One thing finished a moment before the other. Like two brushstrokes, one on top of the other.
And if I were speaking instead of writing?
You'd say: "Quando l'acqua ha smesso di salire, è sceso in strada." Nobody says "ebbe smesso" at the bar. Not even in Florence.
So it's a secret language for books.
More or less. And now tell me the truth: did you like the chapter?
Yes. But something's missing. Grandpa Aldo is in the chapter, but the little girl with the loaf isn't. You must put her in.

Dal libro del professor Bellini: «Il fango e la Madonna»

The book was called "The Mud and the Madonna", and Bellini wrote it in three months, between July and September, in his corner of the workshop, by hand, in black notebooks identical to his grandfather's. The publisher, a small Florentine house specialising in the city's history, wanted to bring it out on 4 November, for the sixtieth anniversary of the flood. The first reader was Pietro, who received the manuscript one Saturday morning with a single instruction: "Read it and tell me the truth. If you get bored, stop." Pietro didn't stop. He read it all in one night. This is how it began.

"It had been raining for three days. It was 3 November 1966, and Florence was going to sleep like every evening, not knowing it would not wake up in the same city. Ernesto Bellini was sixty-two, had a restoration workshop in Via Maggio and a two-year-old grandson asleep in the next room. That evening he worked late on a small fourteenth-century Madonna, then turned off the lamp, locked the door with the big iron key and went upstairs. Before going to bed he looked out of the window. The Arno was higher than usual, dark and fast. Ernesto thought the rain would stop the next day. He was wrong."

"At two in the morning he was woken by a noise he had never heard before: a long, deep roar, as if the city were breathing under water. Ernesto got up, lit a candle, because the electricity had already gone, and went downstairs. When he reached the bottom, the water was already up to his ankles. It was cold, brown, full of floating things: chairs, bottles, a hat, a canary's empty cage. Ernesto understood in an instant what was happening. He ran towards the workshop. But as soon as he had turned the key in the lock, the water flung the door open and pushed him back."

"All night the water rose. Ernesto watched it rise from the first-floor window, his grandson in his arms, helpless. It rose over the doors, over the ground-floor windows, over the shop signs. In the workshop beneath him were forty years of work: canvases, panels, brushes, paints, his father's notebooks. Towards dawn the grandson woke up and asked, in his little two-year-old voice, why the street had become a river. Ernesto didn't know what to answer. He told him only: 'Look carefully, because one day you'll tell this story.'"

Pietro stopped at that line and looked up at Bellini, who was reading the paper and pretending not to watch him. "The grandson is you," he said. Bellini nodded without looking up. "I don't remember it," he replied. "I was two. But my grandfather told me about it so many times that now I feel I remember it. And that's why I used the passato remoto. It's not something I saw. It's something I was told. The passato remoto is the tense of other people's stories."

"On the morning of 4 November," the book went on, "once the water had stopped rising, Ernesto went down into the street. The city he saw was no longer Florence. It was a sea of mud, a metre deep, covering everything: cars, pavements, shops. The smell was terrible, of fuel oil and rotten things. People came out of their houses with grey faces, without speaking. A woman was crying, sitting on a step. An old man was trying to pull a bicycle out of the mud. Ernesto walked to the church of San Frediano with mud up to his knees, and once he had gone in, he stopped in the doorway and started crying too."

"On the side altar, where for three hundred years there had been a small Madonna painted on wood, the water had risen two metres. The Madonna was still in her place, but the mud had covered her hands and the child she held in her arms. The wood was already swelling. Ernesto knew that unless they carried it away within a few days, the panel would split. But it was too heavy for one man of sixty-two. He looked around. There was nobody in the church. For two days Ernesto came back every morning, alone, to look at it without being able to touch it. On the third day he heard, outside, the bell of a bicycle."

"It was a tall, very thin young man with hair that was too long and a red bicycle covered in mud up to the handlebars. His name was Aldo, he said, he came from Bologna, he had come by train as far as Prato, because Florence station was closed, and had cycled to the Oltrarno. Ernesto pointed to the Madonna without saying anything. The young man understood. He leaned the bicycle against the wall, waded into the mud up to his waist and took the heavier end of the panel. Ernesto took the other. It took them an hour to carry it out, one step at a time, without ever letting it fall. Once they had laid it on a dry table, in a house nearby, they sat on the floor and laughed like two madmen."

"The young man stayed in Florence for three weeks. He worked with Ernesto every day, from dawn to dusk, cleaning canvases, washing frames, carrying buckets of clean water from the fountain in Piazza Santo Spirito. He slept on a camp bed in the workshop, among the panels laid out to dry. On 14 November he arrived late, and when Ernesto had asked him why, he answered that he had stopped in Via Maggio, in front of a trattoria full of mud. He said nothing more. When, at the end of the month, the time had come to leave, Ernesto gave him his biggest brush, the one with blue bristles, which he used for skies. 'For when you have a sky to paint,' he told him. The young man put it in his rucksack next to the bread and cycled off to the station."

Pietro read that page three times. Then he took a pencil and, in the margin, in his smallest handwriting, wrote a question: "And the little girl?" When Bellini got the manuscript back, he saw the note and smiled. "I know," he said. "She's missing. But I don't know how to write her. I wasn't there, and my grandfather never saw her. The only one who can tell it is your grandmother." Pietro thought for a moment. "Then ask her," he said. "But ask her to tell it in the passato remoto. Like a true story."

So, one September evening, after the trattoria had closed, Graziella sat down at the table by the window with Bellini, a recorder and a cup of camomile tea. Pietro sat in a corner, silent, with his notebook. At first Graziella spoke in the passato prossimo, the way you speak in the kitchen: "I was twelve, I saw a young man…" Bellini gently stopped her. "Graziella, try to tell it as if it were a fairy tale. The way you'd tell it to Viola." Graziella closed her eyes. Then she began again, in another voice, slower, older.

"Once upon a time there was a twelve-year-old girl who was hungry. For days there had been nothing hot in her parents' trattoria, because the mud had put out the stoves and carried away the flour. Her mother was crying, her father was shovelling, and the little girl sat on the doorstep looking at the street. On the morning of 14 November a young man went by on a red bicycle covered in dirt. When he had seen her, he stopped. He said nothing. He opened his rucksack, took out a loaf, broke it in two and gave her half. Then, as soon as she had taken it, he got back on his bicycle and rode off towards San Frediano."

"The little girl ate the bread sitting on the step, slowly, a piece at a time, because she wanted it to last. It was the best bread she had ever eaten. She didn't know the young man's name, nor where he came from. She thought she would never see him again. Eight years later, one day in March, the young man came into the trattoria, sat at the table by the window and ordered a ribollita. She didn't recognise him. He did. But he didn't tell her. He wrote it to her in twelve letters, which she read fifty years later."

When Graziella had finished, nobody spoke. The recorder kept running in the silence. Pietro had stopped writing long before. Bellini took off his glasses and cleaned them slowly with his tie, as he did when he didn't want anyone to see his eyes. "Graziella," he said at last, "this is the best chapter in the book. And I didn't write it." Graziella shrugged. "Aldo wrote it," she replied. "I only read it aloud."

Marco read the chapter the next day, in the transcript Bellini had typed up on the computer. He read it standing up in the kitchen while his mother was making the soffritto, and when he had finished he said nothing. He went and sat on the trattoria doorstep, the same step as in 1966, and stayed there ten minutes with the sheet in his hand. Graziella watched him from the window without disturbing him. Then Marco came back in, hugged her from behind as he used to as a boy, and said only: "Mum, you'd never told it to me like that." Graziella went on stirring the soffritto. "Because you'd never asked me in the passato remoto," she replied. "In the passato prossimo things seem small. In the remoto they become true."

Davide read the manuscript too, a page a day, in the afternoons, at the big table in the workshop. When he reached the chapter about the mud angels, he stopped and went home earlier than usual. In the evening he came back with an old black-and-white photograph his mother kept in a drawer: a young man with a shovel in his hand and trousers muddy up to the knees, in front of Santa Croce. "It's my grandfather," he told Bellini. "Mum's father. He came from Sardinia in '66, at nineteen. Then he fell in love with a girl from San Frediano and never went back." Bellini looked at the photo for a long time. Then he asked Davide if he could put it in the book, next to the chapter. Davide said yes, blushing to the tips of his ears.

The following Sunday, on the usual video call with Malta, Pietro read the chapter about the loaf aloud to Giulia and Matei, slowly, as Graziella had. Giulia listened sitting on the terrace, with Viola asleep in her arms. When Pietro had finished, Giulia was silent, then said something that surprised everyone. "The blue brush," she said. "The sky brush, which Ernesto gave to Aldo. Tomorrow I'll use it too. In the sky of Caravaggio's painting there's a crack I couldn't close." "But the brush is here in Florence, in Grandma's drawer," said Pietro. Giulia smiled. "Then someone will have to bring it to me." Graziella, behind Pietro, had already picked up her bag.

The chapter went into the book just as it was, word for word, with a single title: "The Loaf". Bellini put it in the middle of the book, between the chapter about the Madonna and the one about the mud angels. Under the title he added a note: "Told by Graziella, transcribed by the author without changing a comma. It is the only chapter in the book in which the narrator was present." When the publisher read it, he phoned Bellini at eleven at night to tell him he had cried on the train in front of everyone. Bellini replied that it often happened, with that trattoria's stories.

Only the dedication remained. Bellini thought about it for days. He tried dedicating the book to his grandfather Ernesto, but it seemed too obvious. He tried Aldo, but Aldo wouldn't have wanted it. He tried Florence, but Florence was too big. In the end, one Saturday morning, as he watched Davide drawing at the big table and Pietro acting as a guide for the tourists at the door, he understood. He took the black notebook and wrote the dedication in a single line, in the passato remoto, like the rest of the book.

"To Pietro and Davide, who read this story before anyone else, and who will one day tell it to someone else." When Pietro saw it, on the proofs that arrived from the publisher at the end of September, he was silent for a long time. Then he said only: "'Lessero' is passato remoto." "I know," replied Bellini. "Because in sixty years, when someone reads this book, you two will already have become a story. Like Ernesto. Like Aldo. Like the little girl with the loaf." Pietro thought for a moment. "Then I'll have to try hard," he said. "A story has to be good, if it ends up in a book."

Davide, when he read the dedication, said nothing. But that afternoon he stayed late in the workshop, and the next day he brought Bellini a drawing. It was the book's cover: a small Madonna lifted by two hands, one old and one young, above a sea of mud, and in a corner, almost hidden, a red bicycle leaning against a wall. Bellini looked at it for a long time. Then he phoned the publisher and told him the cover had changed. The publisher protested that it was too late. Bellini replied that, however late it was, some covers can't be refused. The book came out on 4 November with Davide's drawing.

An excerpt from another chapter of Bellini's book. Read it and answer.
They came from all over Italy and from half of Europe: students, workers, young people who had never seen Florence.
As soon as they had got off the trains, they took a shovel and set to work, without asking for anything.
They slept in churches, ate bread and cheese, shovelled twelve hours a day.
The Florentines called them "mud angels". Many of them, once they had finished, went home and never spoke of it again.
